lesson.title: The Two-Sided Limit: When Both Directions Agree
lesson.summary: The ordinary, unrestricted limit exists only when its left-hand and right-hand counterparts agree on the same value, and the floor function versus the parabola shows exactly what that agreement, and its absence, looks like.
lesson.body:
The plain limit notation lim(x to a) f(x), with no plus or minus mark, is often called the two-sided limit to distinguish it clearly from its one-sided relatives. It is the limit you have been building toward this whole time: the claim that f(x) approaches one single number L as x approaches a from either direction, left or right, with no restriction on which side the input comes from.

The two-sided limit is defined directly in terms of the two one-sided limits you can already compute: lim(x to a) f(x) exists and equals L exactly when both lim(x to a-) f(x) and lim(x to a+) f(x) exist and are equal to the same value L. If the left-hand and right-hand limits disagree, or if either one fails to exist, the two-sided limit simply does not exist at all; there is no averaging or splitting the difference.

Revisit the floor function, f(x) = floor(x), at a = 2. The previous two sections established lim(x to 2-) floor(x) = 1 and lim(x to 2+) floor(x) = 2. Since 1 is not equal to 2, the two one-sided limits disagree, and so lim(x to 2) floor(x) does not exist. This matches the picture: the floor function's graph genuinely jumps at x = 2, so there is no single number that the outputs approach regardless of direction.

Now revisit f(x) = x^2 at a = 2, where the previous section found lim(x to 2-) x^2 = 4 and lim(x to 2+) x^2 = 4. Since both one-sided limits equal 4, the two-sided limit exists and lim(x to 2) x^2 = 4. This matches the picture too: the parabola is smooth and unbroken at x = 2, with no jump for either direction of approach to disagree about.

One more example shows the matching test giving a clean "yes." For f(x) = |x| at a = 0: from the left, x is negative, so |x| = -x, and as x approaches 0-, -x approaches 0. From the right, x is positive, so |x| = x, and as x approaches 0+, x approaches 0. Both one-sided limits equal 0, so lim(x to 0) |x| = 0, even though the absolute value function has a sharp corner at x = 0. A corner is a change in slope, not a jump in value, and the two-sided limit test only cares about the second thing; it says nothing about how smoothly a graph turns.

This left-right matching test is the single most reliable tool for detecting where a limit fails to exist, and it works whether the disagreement comes from a jump (like the floor function), an asymptote where one or both sides run off to infinity, or a piecewise definition with mismatched formulas on either side of a. Whenever a two-sided limit computation feels uncertain, or a function looks suspicious near the target point, splitting the problem into its left-hand and right-hand pieces and comparing them directly, exactly as done here, is the dependable way to settle the question, and it is a habit worth keeping even after faster algebraic shortcuts become available later on.
